thread.title: QYLD: Considering A Different Strategy - Horizons NASDAQ 100 Covered Call ETF (NASDAQ:QYLD)

author: D.M. Martins Research
title: QYLD: Considering A Different Strategy - Horizons NASDAQ 100 Covered Call ETF (NASDAQ:QYLD)
text:
Interest rates have been rising. Volatility in equities has picked up. With the recent, broad-based drop in stock prices, dividend yields have been inching forward.
After nearly a decade of low income (i.e. very little paid to holders of interest-bearing instruments) and a growth bias in the markets, the current landscape is starting to look a bit more favorable for option-writing investment strategies. Morningstar describes the approach as follows:
A typical fund holds a long equity position (DMMR note: ideally on rich-yielding issues), sells in-the-money calls on the reference asset to enhance yield in the portfolio, and buys out-of-the-money puts for some limited downside protection.
Credit: HML Investments
Here's a simple example.
Investor Jane buys 100 shares of Apple ( AAPL ) at $165 each and a current dividend yield of 1.7%. She also sells one call option contract at a strike price of $170 that expires in January 2020 (i.e. in 13 months), collecting a premium of $1,925 today. She uses part of the premium to buy a put option contract with the same expiration date and a strike price of $135 that ensures maximum downside of 18%, paying for it $761. By January 2020, Jane will have collected dividends of $281 plus a net option premium of $1,164, for a total annualized yield on the investment of 8%. In exchange for the attractive payout on such a high-quality stock, she (1) exposes herself to loss of capital from a potential depreciation in AAPL of no more than 18% in a year, and (2) gives up on most of the upside opportunity, should the market value of AAPL increase in the next 12 months.
The approach seems more appropriate for income-seeking investors - for example, retirees looking to "milk" their assets rather than to grow them over time. However, I believe those shooting for moderate growth also could take advantage of the strategy by dripping the dividends and net option premium back into the portfolio, as they are collected.
This covered call investment strategy has been catching my attention lately for the following key reasons:
Higher interest rates typically correlate with higher dividend yields - see graph below. This tends to be true both because (1) companies with a shareholder-friendly dividend policy need to remain competitive against newly-issued fixed income assets that now pay a higher rate of interest, and (2) higher interest also tends to pressure stock value (think of it in terms of a higher discount rate on equity valuation) - and lower asset prices mean higher yields, if all else remains constant. Source: DM Martins Research, using data from multpl.com Stocks have been enduring quite a bit more volatility this year than they did in 2017. By definition, higher expected volatility results in increased option prices. Being a seller when prices are high is, generally speaking, a good investment mantra. An option-writing strategy does not rely on stock prices rising over time, as does a plain-vanilla, buy-and-hold growth approach. In fact, because call options are sold on the shares held in the portfolio, most of the benefit of rising stock prices is not captured by the option-writing investor. The strategy, therefore, can be effective in producing solid results even in an environment of sideways-moving equities. Once upon a time, dealing with an options strategy required more sophistication and a hands-on approach best left for the more seasoned investor. Although a very good understanding of the investment process is still highly advisable, the good news is that cheap ETFs (exchange traded funds) have been allowing the "Average Joe" more access to this investment technique.
I have recently come across Horizons NASDAQ 100 Covered Call ETF ( QYLD ). As of December 2018, this fund had been around for exactly five years. As defined by the management company itself, QYLD tracks a benchmark (the CBOE NASDAQ-100 BuyWrite V2 index) that "measures the total return of a portfolio consisting of equity securities of the 100 companies included in the NASDAQ-100 index and call options systematically written on those securities through a 'buy-write' or covered call strategy." QYLD holds well-known names, including Microsoft ( MSFT ) at an allocation weight of 11%, and even non-dividend paying Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOG )( GOOGL ) that, combined, represent 15% of the total portfolio.
Below is the inception-to-date performance of QYLD compared to that of the Nasdaq index ( QQQ ). To calculate QYLD returns, I used the monthly NAV prices along with the monthly distribution data provided by Horizons. The data provided by Yahoo Finance seems inaccurate, likely the result of the platform's dividend adjustment methodology used to calculate historical share prices.
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from Yahoo Finance and Horizons
There are a few items worth noting from the chart and table above:
Over the past five years, QYLD has performed better than QQQ on a risk-adjusted basis: Sharpe ratio of 0.81 vs. 0.74. QYLD has had higher lows (i.e. better nights of sleep for investors). The fund's worst quarter ever saw a dip of only 5%, whereas the index has lost 14% during the current correction so far. QYLD behaves much more like a moderate growth fund than an aggressive one. Investors with a multi-decade time horizon in mind may miss out on total returns by not investing in a more risk-seeking, stock-only portfolio. Still on the plus side, I find the fund's gross management fee of 0.6% reasonable, given the more complex nature of the investment strategy - and considering how expensive and time consuming it would be for an individual investor to replicate and maintain a similar DIY ("do it yourself") portfolio. Net assets of $403 million and average trading volume of 195,000 further suggest a relatively large and liquid ETF.
On the other hand, QYLD may arguably be too "dumb" an approach that could probably be finessed quite a bit through active management. For example, I may want to explore selling covered calls and buying protective puts with different expiration dates to increase my net premium (or to reduce my risk). Or I may choose not to include names like AMZN in my portfolio, since call writing in this case eliminates perhaps the sole appeal for owning high-growth tech stocks: Capital appreciation.
Still, QYLD seems like a good place to start.
What's next? This is my first peek into the world of covered-option ETFs. These instruments could be well worth the attention as the CBOE's buy-write index had a significantly better risk-reward profile vs. nearly all other major asset classes over the 30-year period ended 2016 (see graph below). While QYLD seems to be an interesting fund worth taking a closer look at, it's only one of many listed by Morningstar under its options-based category.
Source: CBOE
I will likely spend a bit more time in the future looking at these ETFs and exploring which may be most appropriate, given a certain investment objective. I will be sure to report my findings here, on Seeking Alpha.
